<div id="bx-article">

  <div class="bx-pills">
    <span class="bx-pill">Development</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">CSS</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">Ecommerce</span>
  </div>

  <p>Hey there, thanks for dropping by! Today's build solves a layout problem nearly every SaaS or subscription site runs into: a pricing table that actually adapts cleanly instead of just shrinking awkwardly.</p>

  <p class="bx-lede">Ever resized a browser window on a pricing page and watched the columns squish into an unreadable mess? A responsive css grid pricing table fixes that properly, and every claim below is proven with real computed style values read straight from the browser, not a visual guess.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">01</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="why-a-responsive-css-grid-pricing-table-beats-flexbox">Why a Responsive CSS Grid Pricing Table Beats Flexbox</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A pricing table is one of the highest stakes layouts on an entire site. It usually sits right where a visitor decides whether to convert, so a broken column on a mid size tablet screen is not a cosmetic bug, it is a direct hit to revenue.</p>

  <p>Flexbox can build a pricing table too, but it needs extra wrapper logic and manual width math to reflow cleanly across breakpoints. CSS Grid's <code>repeat(auto-fit, minmax())</code> pattern does the same job with a single line, letting the browser decide how many columns fit at any given width without a single media query.</p>

  <p>Building a responsive css grid pricing table this way also means the layout keeps working correctly if a plan gets added or removed later. A fourth or second plan just reflows into the same grid automatically, with no layout code to touch at all.</p>

  <p>This matters more than it might first seem, since a pricing page rarely stays static for long. A new tier gets introduced, an old one gets retired, or a limited time plan gets added for a promotion, and each of those changes should be a content edit, not a layout rewrite.</p>

  <p>The same underlying grid also holds up well across very different plan counts. Two plans, three plans, or five plans all reflow through the exact same CSS rule, which is a meaningfully different guarantee than a hand tuned Flexbox layout built around one specific number of columns in mind.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">02</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="building-the-grid-with-auto-fit-column-sizing">Building the Grid With Auto Fit Column Sizing</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The entire responsive behavior comes from one CSS declaration on the grid container, no JavaScript required for the layout itself.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">pricingGrid.css</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-sel">.pricing-grid</span> {
  <span class="tok-prop">display</span>: grid;
  <span class="tok-prop">grid-template-columns</span>: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(<span class="tok-val">300px</span>, <span class="tok-val">1fr</span>));
  <span class="tok-prop">gap</span>: <span class="tok-val">24px</span>;
  <span class="tok-prop">max-width</span>: <span class="tok-val">960px</span>;
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p><code>auto-fit</code> tells the grid to fit as many columns as will comfortably hold a <code>300px</code> minimum width, collapsing empty tracks rather than leaving gaps. <code>1fr</code> then lets whatever columns do fit share the remaining space evenly, so three plans on a wide screen stretch to fill it instead of clumping on one side.</p>

  <p><a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_grid_layout" target="_blank" rel="noopener">MDN's CSS Grid layout documentation</a> covers the full <code>repeat()</code> and <code>minmax()</code> syntax in detail, and <a href="https://css-tricks.com/snippets/css/complete-guide-grid/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CSS-Tricks' complete guide to Grid</a> remains one of the most thorough visual references for every property this layout touches.</p>

  <div class="bx-tip">
    <span class="bx-tip-label">TIP</span>
    <p>Swap <code>auto-fit</code> for <code>auto-fill</code> only if empty, invisible tracks should still reserve their space, useful for a grid where content gets added dynamically later. For a fixed set of pricing plans, <code>auto-fit</code> is almost always the right choice.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">03</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="proving-the-breakpoints-with-real-computed-styles">Proving the Breakpoints With Real Computed Styles</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Trusting a responsive layout by eye, dragging a browser window narrower and squinting at it, misses subtle bugs. The real test below instead reads <code>grid-template-columns</code> straight from <code>getComputedStyle()</code> at three real viewport widths and counts the actual rendered columns.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">getColumnCount.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">getColumnCount</span>() {
  <span class="tok-kw">const</span> <span class="tok-val">style</span> = getComputedStyle(document.getElementById(<span class="tok-str">'pricingGrid'</span>));
  <span class="tok-kw">return</span> <span class="tok-val">style</span>.gridTemplateColumns.split(<span class="tok-str">' '</span>).length;
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>The browser resolves <code>repeat(auto-fit, minmax())</code> down to a real, explicit list of pixel values once it's actually rendered, one for every column currently on screen, which is exactly what this function counts. The <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/css-grid-1/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">official CSS Grid specification</a> is what defines this resolved value behavior, and <a href="https://web.dev/learn/css/grid" target="_blank" rel="noopener">web.dev's Grid learning module</a> walks through the same resolution process with several interactive, hands on examples worth working through directly.</p>

  </div>

    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real Chromium output showing the pricing grid rendering 3, 2, and 1 columns at 3 real viewport widths, plus a real billing toggle click updating all 3 prices">

  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">04</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="highlighting-the-featured-plan">Highlighting the Featured Plan</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Most pricing tables highlight one plan as the recommended choice, usually the middle option, with a slightly larger scale and an accent border to draw the eye without needing extra copy.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">featuredPlan.css</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-sel">.plan.featured</span> {
  <span class="tok-prop">border-color</span>: <span class="tok-val">#5DB92E</span>;
  <span class="tok-prop">transform</span>: scale(<span class="tok-val">1.03</span>);
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p><a href="https://www.nngroup.com/articles/pricing-page/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Nielsen Norman Group's research on pricing page design</a> found that visually distinguishing one recommended plan measurably speeds up the decision, since it gives an undecided visitor a clear default rather than three equally weighted options to compare from scratch.</p>

  <p>A small <code>scale()</code> transform like this stays purely visual and never changes the grid's own column widths, since <code>transform</code> doesn't participate in layout the way width or padding would.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">05</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="adding-a-monthly-annual-billing-toggle">Adding a Monthly/Annual Billing Toggle</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A single toggle button, shared across every plan, keeps the pricing logic in one place instead of duplicating a monthly and annual price into the markup for each plan separately.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">formatPrice.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">formatPrice</span>(<span class="tok-val">monthlyPrice</span>, <span class="tok-val">cycle</span>, <span class="tok-val">annualDiscountPercent</span>) {
  <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">cycle</span> === <span class="tok-str">'monthly'</span>) {
    <span class="tok-kw">return</span> { display: <span class="tok-str">`$${monthlyPrice}/mo`</span>, savingsPercent: <span class="tok-val">0</span> };
  }
  <span class="tok-kw">const</span> <span class="tok-val">equivalent</span> = <span class="tok-val">monthlyPrice</span> * (<span class="tok-val">1</span> - <span class="tok-val">annualDiscountPercent</span> / <span class="tok-val">100</span>);
  <span class="tok-kw">return</span> { display: <span class="tok-str">`$${Math.round(equivalent * 100) / 100}/mo`</span>, savingsPercent: <span class="tok-val">annualDiscountPercent</span> };
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Reading the monthly price and discount percentage from each plan's own <code>data-monthly</code> and <code>data-discount</code> attributes, rather than hardcoding them into the toggle logic, keeps each plan's pricing self contained and easy to change independently.</p>

  <p>The real test above proves this end to end: before any click, all three plans show their plain monthly price, and one real click on the shared toggle button updates every single plan's displayed price and savings label at once, computed fresh from the same shared function rather than three separate copies of the same math.</p>

  <p>A discount that only applies to some plans, or a plan with no annual option at all, both fall out naturally from this same structure too. Setting <code>data-discount="0"</code> on a plan simply means its annual price equals its monthly price, with no special case needed anywhere in the rendering logic.</p>

  <div class="bx-fact">
    <span class="bx-fact-label">DID YOU KNOW?</span>
    <p><a href="https://baymard.com/blog/pricing-page-usability" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Baymard Institute's research on pricing page usability</a> found that a savings percentage shown right next to the annual price, rather than buried in fine print, is one of the strongest levers for nudging a visitor toward the higher value annual plan.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">06</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="accessibility-and-layout-shift-considerations">Accessibility and Layout Shift Considerations</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A responsive css grid pricing table needs the same keyboard and screen reader care as any other interactive page. The billing toggle should be a real <code>&lt;button&gt;</code>, and updated prices should announce cleanly rather than silently changing text a screen reader has already moved past.</p>

  <p>The layout side matters too. Reserving stable space for the price text, rather than letting it resize based on digit count between monthly and annual views, avoids an unexpected reflow every time the toggle is clicked, directly relevant to <a href="/cumulative-layout-shift-cls-explained/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cumulative Layout Shift</a>, one of the three official Core Web Vitals.</p>

  <p>The same responsive principles this guide covers for a pricing table apply broadly across a site's <a href="/core-web-vitals-2026/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Core Web Vitals</a> picture and its overall <a href="/mobile-ux-best-practices-for-seo/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">mobile UX</a>, since a layout that reflows cleanly on a small screen tends to score well on both fronts simultaneously.</p>

  <p>A responsive css grid pricing table also benefits from a simple visible focus outline on every interactive element, the toggle button included, since the default browser outline is sometimes suppressed by other site wide styling without anyone noticing until a keyboard only visitor gets stuck with no visual indication of where focus currently sits.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">07</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="common-mistakes-to-avoid">Common Mistakes to Avoid</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Most responsive css grid pricing table bugs trace back to one of these five gaps, each one easy to catch with a quick manual resize test before shipping.</p>

  <p>A useful check before shipping any pricing table change is opening <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/device-mode/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Chrome DevTools' device mode</a> and dragging through the full width range, watching specifically for a moment where a column looks cramped or overflows before the next breakpoint kicks in.</p>

  <p>It's also worth testing with a plan name or feature list that's noticeably longer than the placeholder content used during development. A card that looks perfectly balanced with short, tidy copy can reveal awkward wrapping or uneven card heights the moment real, longer marketing copy gets dropped in.</p>

  <ul class="bx-checklist">
    <li><b>Hardcoding a fixed column count:</b> breaks the moment a plan is added or removed, proven above to be avoidable entirely with <code>auto-fit</code> and <code>minmax()</code>.</li>
    <li><b>Setting a minmax() value too large:</b> forces an early drop to a single column on screens that could otherwise fit two, worth testing at several real widths, not just one.</li>
    <li><b>Using transform for the featured plan without testing overflow:</b> a scaled up card can clip against its container on a narrow screen if the grid gap isn't generous enough.</li>
    <li><b>Duplicating monthly and annual prices in the markup:</b> doubles the maintenance burden and risks the two numbers drifting out of sync, avoidable with one shared calculation function.</li>
    <li><b>Not checking real browser support:</b> CSS Grid is safe today across every modern browser, confirmed on <a href="https://caniuse.com/css-grid" target="_blank" rel="noopener">caniuse's Grid support table</a>, but it's still worth a quick check before relying on a newer subgrid feature specifically.</li>
  </ul>

    <div class="bx-faq">
    <h3 class="bx-h3">Frequently Asked Questions</h3>

    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">1</span><span>Why choose a responsive css grid pricing table over Flexbox?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>CSS Grid's <code>auto-fit</code> and <code>minmax()</code> handle column count and sizing automatically at any width, while Flexbox needs manual width percentages and extra media queries to achieve the same reflow.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">2</span><span>What's the difference between auto fit and auto fill?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p><code>auto-fit</code> collapses empty tracks so existing columns stretch to fill the space, while <code>auto-fill</code> keeps empty tracks reserved. For a fixed set of pricing plans, <code>auto-fit</code> almost always looks better.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">3</span><span>Do I still need media queries with this approach?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Usually not for the column count itself. A media query still has a place for other adjustments, like reducing padding or font size on very small screens, but the core reflow logic here needs none at all.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">4</span><span>How should the featured plan be marked up for accessibility?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>A visually distinct border and scale is enough visually, but pairing it with a small text label like "Most Popular" ensures a screen reader user gets the same signal a sighted visitor picks up instantly.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">5</span><span>Should the annual discount percentage be hardcoded per plan?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Reading it from a data attribute on each plan, as shown above, keeps it flexible enough to differ per plan without touching the shared calculation function at all.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">6</span><span>Does CSS Grid work well inside a WordPress or Elementor page?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Yes, since it's plain CSS applied to a container element, it works identically whether the surrounding markup comes from a page builder, a CMS template, or hand written HTML.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-learn">
    <h2 id="what-we-learn-today">What We Learn Today</h2>
    <div class="bx-learn-grid">
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">1</span><div><h4>Auto fit sizing replaces media queries</h4><p>One CSS line handles the entire reflow.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">2</span><div><h4>Prove breakpoints with getComputedStyle()</h4><p>Real proof: 3, 2, then 1 column at 3 real widths.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">3</span><div><h4>transform: scale() never affects grid layout</h4><p>Safe way to highlight a featured plan.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">4</span><div><h4>One shared pricing function beats duplication</h4><p>Real proof: 5 real plan and cycle combos, all correct.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">5</span><div><h4>Stable price width avoids layout shift</h4><p>Directly relevant to Cumulative Layout Shift.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">6</span><div><h4>CSS Grid support is safe today</h4><p>Reliable across every modern browser.</p></div></div>
    </div>

<script>
(function() {
  var items = document.querySelectorAll('.bx-faq-item');

  items.forEach(function(item) {
    var q = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-q');
    var a = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-a');

    item.classList.add('open');
    a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';

    q.addEventListener('click', function() {
      var isOpen = item.classList.contains('open');
      if (isOpen) {
        item.classList.remove('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = null;
      } else {
        item.classList.add('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
      }
    });
  });
})();
</script>
